glossary.definition: The city's main operating fund. Money here is unrestricted — the Council can spend it on almost any city purpose (police, fire, parks, admin). This is where the ~$30M structural deficit lives.

An ongoing, recurring gap where normal expenses exceed normal revenues year after year — as opposed to a one-time shortfall. It doesn't go away on its own and can't be permanently fixed with one-time money.
Money available only once — e.g., reserves, a fund transfer, sale proceeds. Useful to bridge a single year but dangerous to rely on for recurring costs, because the gap reappears next year.
The starting-point budget built from actual spending and service needs BEFORE any proposed cuts. The FY27-28 plan rebuilt baselines from actual expenditures rather than prior budgets.
The final budget formally approved by the City Council. The FY25-26 biennial budget is current; the FY27-28 biennial budget was adopted June 23, 2026.
The City Manager's recommended budget before Council adoption — subject to change through hearings.
A two-year budget. Berkeley budgets in two-year cycles with a mid-cycle update.
A check-in partway through. 'Mid-year' here = first half of the fiscal year (Jul–Dec). 'Mid-biennial' = the update between the two years of a biennial budget.
Berkeley's budget year runs July 1 – June 30. 'FY2026' = July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026. 'FY2027' begins July 1, 2026.
A fund for a service expected to pay for itself through its own fees/charges (e.g., Marina berths, parking). When it can't, the General Fund covers the difference.
Money legally restricted to a specific purpose, often from a dedicated tax or grant (e.g., Measure P for homelessness, Parks Tax). Can't be freely redirected.
A fund where one city department 'charges' others for shared services (e.g., IT, building maintenance, workers' comp). Revenue comes from internal transfers.
The multi-year plan for big physical projects — streets, sidewalks, buildings, docks. Separate from day-to-day operating costs. Berkeley's is a 5-year plan, updated each biennium.
The actionable, appropriated portion of the CIP — actual funding for that year's projects. Years 3-5 are planning estimates only.
A future obligation the city owes (mainly pensions and retiree health / OPEB) for which it has NOT yet set aside enough money. Grows or shrinks with investment returns and assumptions.
Other Post-Employment Benefits — chiefly retiree health care, separate from pensions. Often lumped with pensions in 'unfunded liabilities.'
Assets ÷ liabilities for the pension plan. 100% = fully funded. Berkeley was ~66% (FY2020), which the state classified as 'high risk.'
Eliminating positions — both layoffs of filled jobs and removal of vacant (unfilled) positions.
A way to count staffing where 1.0 = one full-time position. Two half-time staff = 1.0 FTE. Lets the city compare headcount consistently.
Vacant = budgeted but no one in the seat (cheaper to cut — no layoff). Filled = an actual employee, so cutting means a layoff.

Positions/offices established by the City Charter and somewhat independent of the City Manager: City Attorney, City Auditor, the Director of Police Accountability (ODPA), and the Mayor & Council. They set their own reductions first.
Departments under the City Manager's authority (Police, Fire, Public Works, etc.) — distinct from Charter offices.
Proposed 0.5% local sales-tax increase for the Nov 2026 ballot. Would raise ~$9.0–9.4M/yr, bring Berkeley to 10.75%, and (if passed) reduce the depth of cuts. Needs simple majority.
Borrowing repaid through a dedicated property tax. Needs 2/3 voter approval. The proposed $300M infrastructure bond is a GO bond.
Voter-approved ~$270M, 14-year funding stream (~$15M/yr) for streets, sidewalks, safety, and environmental work ('Safe Streets').
Voter-approved $100M infrastructure bond, now fully allocated across two phases.
Property-transfer-tax measure funding homelessness services; currently spending more than it brings in.
Tax measure supporting affordable housing; finance staff note it ultimately 'rolls up to' the General Fund.
The entity winding down the dissolved Redevelopment Agency. Its liquidation produces a one-time $7.88M transfer to the city used in the FY27-28 bridge.
Money moved between funds. In the GF revenue tab, the large FY26 transfers increase reflects the Successor Agency dissolution and reserve movements.
Accounting that records money when cash actually changes hands (vs accrual, which records when earned/owed). The mid-year revenue report is on this basis.
Savings set aside for emergencies or smoothing. Drawing them down is a one-time fix. Berkeley's GF available cash fell from $85.4M to $30.6M between 2023 and 2025.
0–100 score of street quality. Berkeley targets a citywide PCI of 70, ideally no street below 50.
Mid-year actual ÷ full-year adopted budget. Around 50% mid-year is roughly on pace; well above/below flags timing or trend issues.
The proposed dollar reduction ÷ that department's baseline budget — i.e., how deep the cut is in percentage terms.
One-time money assigned to a department to soften its cut in FY27 while awaiting the Nov 2026 sales-tax vote. Mainly Police, Fire, and PRW.
A tax set at a fixed amount for each parcel of property (or for each room or square foot). A local government needs two-thirds of voters to approve one.
glossary.quote: With the approval of two-thirds of voters, local governments may impose a tax on all parcels in their jurisdiction (or a subset of parcels in their jurisdiction). Local governments typically set parcel taxes at fixed amounts per parcel (or fixed amounts per room or per square foot of the parcel).

questions.question: Where does my property tax go?

paragraphs.text: The basic 1% property tax is pooled by the county and divided under state law among the county, cities, schools and [special districts](glossary:Special district).

cites.quote: Your county auditor pools your 1 percent rate tax payment, as well as payments from other property owners in your county, into a single countywide pot.
State law directs how your county auditor distributes the revenue in the countywide pot.
your county auditor sets aside this $1,000 for your city, county, schools, and special districts.

paragraphs.text: On top of that, voters approve extra taxes for particular governments, and that money goes to them, not the City. BUSD's three school [parcel taxes](glossary:Parcel tax) bring in $68.8M in 2026-27.

cites.quote: The second largest funding source comes from local parcel tax Measures, which provide a total of $68.8 million

paragraphs.text: Berkeley's public schools are run by Berkeley Unified School District (BUSD), a separate government with its own budget: $248.2 million of General Fund revenue in 2026-27. [See BUSD's budget, explained](page:schools).

cites.quote: For the 2026-27 fiscal year, the Berkeley Unified School District's (BUSD) combined General Fund is projected to receive $248.2 million in revenue

paragraphs.text: Staff costs are most of the General Fund: the City cites {fig:personnelAndPension.personnelSubtotal} for personnel, of a {fig:personnelAndPension.compositionTotal} General Fund. That's {fig:personnelAndPension.composition.0} in salaries and {fig:personnelAndPension.composition.1} in pension, health and other benefits, which the City reports together.
For unfunded liabilities, staff have recently cited about {fig:personnelAndPension.unfundedLiabilities.2}. Estimates vary with how and when they're measured.

In {year}, the capital program pays for streets from the General Fund, {fig:capitalProgram.lines.1.years.2027} for street condition improvement and {fig:capitalProgram.lines.0.years.2027} for other street work, and from funds that can only go to transportation: Measure BB sales tax, {fig:capitalProgram.lines.10.years.2027}; the state gas tax, {fig:capitalProgram.lines.12.years.2027}; and the vehicle registration fee, {fig:capitalProgram.lines.11.years.2027}. Measure FF (Safe Streets) adds {fig:capitalProgram.lines.17.years.2027}.
The City estimates its unfunded capital and maintenance needs, streets included, at {fig:documentFacts.capitalNeed}. See the [Capital page](page:capital).

questions.question: What would the sales tax measure change?

paragraphs.text: Measure V would add a general sales tax in Berkeley. The City estimates it would bring in $9 to $10 million a year, starting April 1, 2027, and as a general tax its money would go into the General Fund.

cites.quote: CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE V
The City estimates the tax will generate $9 to $10 million annually.
the tax would go into effect beginning April 1, 2027, and last until ended by the voters
This would be a general tax, meaning the revenue from the tax would be placed into the General Fund and could be spent on any valid municipal purpose.

paragraphs.text: [See the budget with and without it](page:ballot).

questions.question: Who pays the most property tax?

paragraphs.text: The City's financial report lists the ten largest property owners by taxable assessed value. In 2025 the largest was Bayer Healthcare LLC, at 1.56% of the taxable value of all real property in the City; the top ten together were 5.79%.
